extracted.intended_audience: educators, instructional designers, and researchers interested in e-learning and educational philosophy (higher-education practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for educators on how philosophical orientations of teaching and technology should inform the selection and use of e‑learning technologies. Describes major technology-determinism positions and teaching philosophies and explains their implications for practice and technology choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation of personal philosophy-in-practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing and articulating one's philosophy of teaching and technology — a conceptual framework embodying certain values from which we view education and e‑learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing your personal philosophy helps you understand why you act and think the way you do about using e‑learning technologies, why others act differently, and the consequences of technological choices. It facilitates setting learner expectations, determining purpose and outcomes, and communicating not only what you are doing but why (Draper, 1993; Darkenwald & Merriam, 1982; Zinn, 1990). Many educators' philosophies are implicit; making them explicit can improve effectiveness when choosing/using e‑learning tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses determinism (technology as neutral tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies are perceived as neutral tools whose effects are determined by how users employ them; the focus is on technological uses and user agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated scholars: Fiske; Jonassen (1996); Clark (1983, 1985). Example claims: 'computers should be used as tools for helping learners build knowledge; they should not control the learner' (Jonassen). Advantages: affirms individual control and autonomy over technology; aligns with practitioner-focused instructional strategy. Pitfalls/anti-patterns: can produce instrumentalism (assuming a technological fix), overemphasis on actor intentionality, neglect of social structures and the embedding of systems, and naïve belief in complete user control. Practically, educators adopting this view may favor technologies that extend existing instructional strategies (e.g., course management systems used to deliver designed instruction) but should be cautious about ignoring systemic or structural effects of technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social determinism (technology shaped by social context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological artefacts and their forms/uses are shaped by social systems, cultures, and social choices; technology is socially embedded and constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated scholars: Golding & Murdock; Woolgar; Schiller. Examples/pundits: some e‑learning futurists who argue market/social forces will transform providers (e.g., Drucker, Ellison, Lanier). Implications: Emphasizes how social context shapes both form and content of learning experiences; calls attention to institutional, cultural, and economic drivers. Pitfalls/anti-patterns: can underplay user control and material limits if taken exclusively; may lead to flawed understanding if user agency and technological affordances are ignored. Practitioners should examine institutional and cultural influences when adopting technologies while also recognizing mutual shaping between users, society, and technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological determinism (technology as causal agent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies are viewed as causal forces that determine uses and drive social change; technology itself has pivotal social effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated scholars: McLuhan, Postman, Marcuse, Winner; historically linked to Marxist analyses (e.g., Mumford). This orientation can be framed negatively (technology as instrument of domination, commodification of education) or positively (technology transforms and can improve learning). Examples: claims that media reshape society ('the medium is the message'); views that asynchronous text tools can foster higher-order reflection (e.g., Lapadat; Garrison & Anderson). Pitfalls: overemphasis on technology's independence can ignore social/user embeddedness and historical forces. Practitioners should recognize significant technological impacts and unanticipated consequences while avoiding one-dimensional explanations that ignore social and human factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal/Perennial teaching orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: An orientation aiming to search for truth and develop moral, intellectual, and aesthetic qualities in learners (rooted in classical liberal education).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims: develop rational, intellectual wisdom, moral values, spiritual/aesthetic sensibility. Methods: rigorous intellectual training, emphasis on grammar, rhetoric, great books, lecture followed by dialogue, intuition and contemplation. Role of technology: generally skeptical—aligns most closely with technological determinism in that standardized, modularized automated courses conflict with the liberal aim of deep intellectual development; many textual/asynchronous technologies may conflict with the dialogic, reflective aims. Criticisms: elitism, insufficient attention to vocational subjects and life-related topics. Practitioners with this orientation should be cautious about using e‑learning solutions that prioritize convenience, standardization, or customer-service models over depth and intellectual rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive teaching orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: An orientation focused on personal growth and social improvement; education organized around problems and students' experiences (pragmatist roots: Dewey, James).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims: personal growth, social reform, democratic cooperation. Methods: experiential, problem-solving, curriculum organized around real situations; teacher as organizer/consultant/encourager in partnership with learners. Role of technology: aligns most closely with uses determinism—certain e‑learning technologies (e.g., conferencing in LMS, asynchronous communication) can effectively support learner-centered, democratic interactions, giving equal opportunity to contribute and enabling reflective discourse. Criticisms: may overestimate education's power to effect social change and underplay the role of subject matter or teacher authority. Practitioners should design e‑learning to facilitate collaboration, reflection, and situated problem-solving while attending to facilitation quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviourist teaching orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: An orientation aiming to produce observable changes in behaviour through stated objectives and reinforcement (classic behaviourist methods such as mastery learning, PSI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims: change behaviour to meet societal needs; learning judged by reproducible performance under similar circumstances. Methods: stated learning objectives, rewards/punishments, mastery learning, individually prescribed instruction. Role of technology (implied/practical): well suited to automated, programmed instruction, mastery systems, quizzes and reinforcement mechanisms that track observable performance. Criticisms/anti-patterns: can dehumanize learners, fragment curriculum into bits, inhibit creativity, and neglect incidental or deeper forms of learning. Practitioners should weigh the efficiency and clarity of behaviourist-aligned technologies against risks to holistic learning and learner engagement.
